newsitem.title: REPUBLIC OF IRELAND: Ireland expects tough EU Fisheries Council.
newsitem.headline: Ireland expects tough EU Fisheries Council.

text.p: Ireland's minister for the marine Sean Barrett said on Wednesday that he expected this week's EU Fisheries Council to be "very tough going".

Barrett, who will chair the meeting, said the Council faced into a marathon agenda as Ireland puts on a last big push to make concrete and lasting progress on the major items on the fisheries agenda in addition to delivering agreement on next year's catch allocations.
The Fisheries Council is the last scheduled Council of the Irish presidency which ends on December 31.

"We have a very heavy and difficult agenda this week," Barrett said in a statement. "The scale of the agenda reflects our approach throughout the presidency to fisheries issues which has been to make tangible progress on all current major issues while delivering the normal round of EU fisheries business in an efficient and effective way."

He said the Irish presidency would be battling to broker a compromise deal on the European Commission's proposals for catches for 1997 in the context of pessimistic scientific advice about most EU fish stocks.
Barrett said he would be working to reconcile the conservation imperative with the economic needs of the fish industries as far as possible.

He will also be looking for further progress towards agreeing the Irish Presidency's compromise proposal on reducing the EU fishing effort which was crafted following the rejection of Commissioner Emma Bonino's proposal for 40 percent fleet cuts at the October Council.

"The discussions this week will determine how far member states are prepared to commit themselves and how far the Commission is prepared to concede to political reality at this time," Barrett said, noting that the possible outcomes ranged from political agreement on the Irish text to agreement to take a decision at some firm date next year.
"The EU needs to take responsibilities seriously and deliver a rational targeted and fair solution to the problem to overfishing within a reasonable time frame.
"My objective is to push forward and ensure that the outcome is firmly based on the Irish Presidency solution," Barrett said.
Other issues on the agenda include consideration of new conservation measures and of 11 EU fisheries agreements with other countries, including Norway.
Barrett said he would also launch a debate on the future direction of the EU's Common Fisheries Policy.

"I want to see fishermen, processors and the scientists together with fisheries administrations and the Commission engaging in frank, intensive and comprehensive debate about the Common Fisheries Policy," he said.
